title: Bao Shuya Understood Guan Zhong
text:
In the 7th century BC, in the state of Qi, two young men named Guan Zhong and Bao Shuya were close friends. Sima Qian preserves Guan Zhong's own memory of that friendship. When they traded together, Guan took the larger share of the profits, and Bao did not call him greedy, because he knew Guan was poor. When Guan's plans failed, Bao did not call him foolish, because he knew timing could be against him. When Guan fled from battle three times, Bao did not call him a coward, because he knew Guan had an old mother to support.

Later the two served rival princes in a struggle for the throne of Qi. Guan Zhong even shot an arrow at Bao's master, Prince Xiaobai, and hit his belt buckle. Xiaobai won and became Duke Huan. Guan was captured and seemed sure to die.

Instead Bao Shuya urged the duke to make Guan Zhong his chief minister, and took the lower place himself. Under Guan's government Qi became the leading power among the states. Guan Zhong said: "My parents gave me life, but it is Bao who understood me." The phrase "the friendship of Guan and Bao" is still used in Chinese for a true friendship.
lesson: Judge a friend by his circumstances and his abilities, not by his worst moments. Speaking up for someone's talent, even at your own expense, can change his life.
people: Guan Zhong, Bao Shuya, Duke Huan of Qi
source: Sima Qian, Records of the Grand Historian (Shiji), chapter 62, Biographies of Guan Zhong and Yan Ying
